# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 156)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22). George has departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne; Amelia now walks to Russell Square evenings when George does not visit, resting by garden railing, praying as lights go out in his chamber.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Jos's annuity still paying despite Old Sedley's deception. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gaunt House; Gulton; Bryngate (market town); Lombard Street (bank); Calcutta (Jos); Madras (Major); Mirecombe (hill farms); Brookgreen Fair.
- **Seasonal/environmental details**: Summer—bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; rain threatening since morning but holding off; dog barks and goes quiet; children chase hoop down lane; bells of Sabbath ringing; evenings cool and pleasant.

## Main Characters

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Court presentation achievement (Chapter 21)**: Gained presentation through Lady Jane's sponsorship, pronounced "charmante."
- **Court jewels scheme (Chapter 21)**: Court diamonds hired from Mr. Polonius of Coventry Street; **never returned**. Steyne financed diamonds hidden in Amelia's old desk. Pitt gave diamond clasp; blushed when mentioned.
- **Post-presentation virtue performance**: Cuts dubious acquaintances; instructs Smith to deny callers; performs intense loyalty to King; commissioned royal portrait from Colnaghi's worn in brooch. Narrator notes rouge won't come off; some rouge so good tears won't disturb it.
- **Gaunt House musical triumph (Chapter 21)**: Sang very best; men crowded round piano; women enemies left alone. Paul Jefferson Jones praised her.
- **Prince of Peterwaradin's patronage (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: After visit to Lord Steyne, Prince renewed acquaintance with Rawdon at Club; invited Crawleys to Prince's small party at Levant House. Rebecca sang after dinner to very little comité; Steyne present, "paternally superintending."
- **French diplomatic circle (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Became constant guest at French Embassy; no party considered complete without "charming Madame Ravdonn Cravley." Messieurs de Truffigny (Perigord family) and Champignac, Embassy attachés, declared themselves "au mieux" with her.
- **Social manipulation of professional artists (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Makes conspicuously polite point of being kind to professional ladies and gentlemen at aristocratic parties; follows them to corners, shakes hands in view of all. Frankly acknowledges artistic origin with "frankness and humility" that provokes, disarms, or amuses. Professional personages leave sore throats to sing at her parties and give lessons free.
- **Narrative assessment (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Described variously as "cool," assuming "airs of independence"; "honest and good-natured soul"; "artful little minx." Narrator: "They were all right very likely, but Becky went her own way."
- **Financial transactions (Chapter 21)**: Bank arrangement (Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Lombard Street) providing substantial sum; distributed strategically to Briggs, Raggles, livery-man Spavin.
- **Maternal rejection (unchanged)**: Would have preferred to leave little Rawdon behind.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- **Complete subjugation (unchanged)**: "Beat and cowed into laziness and submission." Bold reckless blood turned torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout.
- **Possible new opportunity (Chapter 22 – CLAIM, not fact)**: Rebecca muses Rawdon "would make a very good Ecuyer--Master of the Ceremonies...the man in the large boots and the uniform, who goes round the ring cracking the whip? He is large, heavy, and of a military figure." Reflects on childhood experience at Brookgreen Fair.
- **Strong attachment to little Rawdon (unchanged)**: Wraps boy in shawls; hoists onto coach roof; walks and rides with brother Pitt.

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- **Post-separation behavior (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Now comes to see mother on pony with coachman, riding proudly with grandfather Sedley down lane. **Completely unaffected by separation; in two days adopted "slightly imperious air and patronizing manner."** Visits little school to show off new wealth and splendour. Mother thinks: "He was born to command, his father was before him." **"He is not her boy any more."** Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."

**Amelia Osborne (Mrs. George Osborne)**
- **Separation complete (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: George departs Russell Square to live with Old Osborne, summer of sixth year. Child elated and eager; mother's heart breaking as he goes smiling away.
- **Daily ritual (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: On evenings when George does not come, takes long walk into London as far as Russell Square; rests on stone by garden railing opposite Mr. Osborne's house. Looks up at drawing-room windows illuminated; at about nine o'clock sees chamber in upper story where Georgy sleeps (he told her). Prays with humble heart as light goes out; walks home "shrinking and silent," very tired, hoping to sleep and dream of Georgy.
- **Church encounter (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: One Sunday walking in Russell Square, bells of Sabbath ringing, saw George and his aunt Miss Osborne leaving for church. Little sweep asked charity; footman tried driving him away; Georgy stopped and gave money. Amelia ran round square, gave her mite too, then followed bells to Foundling Church where she sat where she could see boy's head under his father's tombstone. Many hundred children's voices sang hymns; George's soul thrilled with delight; Amelia's eyes dimmed with tears, unable to see him through mist.
- **Maternal anguish and self-blame (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Made thousand eager declarations about preparations before separation; tears fell into boxes; passages scored in favorite books; old toys, relics, treasures packed with strange care—**boy took no note**. Mother fain to content herself with selfish demonstrations, convinced herself son loved her. Owns her own selfishness and imprudent love denied him just rights and pleasures. Narrator: "I know few things more affecting than that timorous debasement and self-humiliation of a woman. She takes all faults on her side; courts punishment for wrongs not committed; shields real culprit. It is those who injure women who get the most kindness from them."
- **Father's confession (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Old Sedley revealed Jos **still paying annuity** despite appearance of abandonment. Sedley's imprudence flung it away; concealed truth extended period. Confessed with trembling, miserable voice. Amelia fell on neck kissing him many times, crying "You are always good and kind. It is not for the money...my God! my God! have mercy upon me, and give me strength to bear this trial."
- **Letter to Jos (Chapter 21)**: Wrote tender supplication to Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support to parents, painting condition in artless pathos. Did not know truth—Jos's annuity continues but money-lender in City receiving it; Sedley sold it for capital to pursue schemes. Calculated eagerly time before answer arrived.
- **Regarding Major at Madras**: Had not communicated griefs; not written since congratulating on approaching marriage. Thought with sickening despondency only friend who felt such regard was fallen away.
- **Physical and emotional decline (Chapter 21)**: Grows daily more care-worn and sad, fixing alarmed eyes on child. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights.
- **Old desk (unchanged)**: Years ago gave Rebecca desk now containing Rebecca's diamonds and valuables.

**Old Mr. Sedley**
- **Receives hundred pounds (Chapter 22 – UPDATED)**: Amelia kissed him, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands before George's departure, saying "don't be harsh with Georgy. He—he is not going to stop with us long."
- **Financial decline and deception (Chapter 21)**: Dabbled in speculation; wine and coal companies failed; bills in arrear. **Sold Jos's annuity**: Received sum to pursue bootless schemes; concealed from family extended period. Confessed with trembling, miserable voice.

**Miss Osborne (Old Osborne's daughter)**
- **Receives Amelia's letter and capitulates (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Letter made her blush; looked toward glooming father. Next day visited Amelia; meeting friendly. Cold, sensible, not unkind. Poor widow realized no fear lest Miss Osborne take first place in son's affection. Conquered, laying down arms, humbly submitted. That day arranged preliminaries of capitulation treaty.
- **Prepares George's room (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Room unopened 10+ years; contained George's clothes, papers, handkerchiefs, whips, caps, fishing-rods, sporting gear. 1814 Army list with name; little dictionary; Bible mother gave him on mantelpiece with spurs and dried inkstand of ten years' dust. Room symbol of frozen grief. Miss Osborne much affected entering; sank pale on little bed. Housekeeper: "This is blessed news, m'am...good old times returning...dear little feller...but some folks in May Fair, m'am, will owe him grudge, m'am." Housekeeper opened window-sash, letting air into chamber.
- **Seen with George (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: Walks with George to church on Sabbath; observed by Amelia.

**Old Mr. Osborne**
- **Reaction to Amelia's letter (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: When Miss Osborne read with tremulous eager voice, said "What? Mrs. Pride has come down, has she? Reg'lar starved out, hey? Ha, ha! I knew she would." Tried keeping dignity reading paper; could not follow it. Chuckled and swore behind sheet. Commanded: "Get the room over mine--his room that was--ready." Could not suppress satisfaction.

**The Marquis of Steyne**
- **Financing Rebecca's scheme (Chapter 21)**: Present at Court; financed Rebecca's diamonds. Made bank arrangement providing substantial sum. Observed Rebecca sing Mozart at Gaunt House.
- **Pupil supervision (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: At Levant House Prince of Peterwaradin's party, present "paternally superintending the progress of his pupil" (Rebecca).

**Lady Steyne**
- **Musical responsiveness (Chapter 21)**: Held "very highest rank in Vanity Fair"; severe, spotless, beautiful. Moved to tears by Rebecca's Mozart singing.

**Prince of Peterwaradin (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- Renewed acquaintance with Rawdon at Club; gave profound salute in Hyde Park Ring; invited Crawleys to small party at Levant House (then occupied during proprietor's absence from England).

**Duc de la Jabotiere (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- Fine gentleman and greatest minister Europe produced; Ambassador from Most Christian King; subsequently Minister to that monarch. Rebecca met at French Embassy; became constant guest there.

**French Diplomatic Attachés (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- **Messieurs de Truffigny** (Perigord family) and **Champignac**: Both attachés of French Embassy; both "straightway smitten" by Rebecca; both declared themselves "au mieux" with "charming Madame Ravdonn Cravley."

**Minor Characters - Bryngate/Mirecombe (Chapter 22 – NEW)**
- **Madrek Orlwood**: Spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight; never kept promise to rebuild wall at Fenmere.
- **Fedette Orlwood**: Remarked river up again; Feena Stenworth said it always was in spring.
- **Feena Stenworth**: Agreed with Fedette regarding river.
- **Orvie Hollett and Rozek Hollwood**: Daughter Hamira Hollwood born; family lived in Mirecombe.
- **Daric Brackwood**: Laughed at story nobody else found funny.
- **Brenelle Brackwood**: Fell asleep in chair before fire caught.
- **Daric and Nylis Corrett**: Talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.
- **Isnar**: Laughed at story nobody else found funny.

## Critical Facts (Chapters 21–22 – UPDATED)
- **George permanently separated from mother**: Living with Old Osborne at Russell Square; visits mother on pony with coachman; completely unaffected and patronizing toward mother after two days. Amelia walks to Russell Square evenings, prays at his window, attended church to see him. Narrator's judgment: her love for him is "bootless" in Vanity Fair.
- **Rebecca's ascendancy in high society**: Now moving among European diplomatic circles (Prince of Peterwaradin, French Embassy); professional artists compete for her favor; "paternally superintended" by Steyne; described variously as cool, honest-natured, artful minx—all accurate.
- **Steyne's continued control**: Finances Rebecca; supervises her progress; maintains her in dependency through bank arrangements and social patronage.
- **Jos's annuity continues**: Still paying despite Old Sedley's deception and sale to money-lender; family unaware.
- **Narrator's commentary (Chapter 22)**: On Vanity Fair's transitory pleasures (roast beef, aristocratic delights); on mysteries of great world ("As I cannot describe the mysteries of freemasonry...an uninitiated man cannot take upon himself to portray the great world accurately").
